blocks.title: Change 200 files without one 8,000-line diff
blocks.description: Give Astravia the upgrade or the rename. It writes the transform down precisely, measures how far it reaches, then ships it as a tracked migration: one GitHub pull request per batch, CI verified before the next batch starts, progress recorded on one issue.

showcase.user_prompt: Move this repo from jest to vitest.

items.title: The transform, written down
items.description: “Modernize the tests” becomes an exact rule — which call becomes which, which config is renamed, which variants stay untouched — so every batch applies the same decision.

items.title: Scope measured first
items.description: It counts the files before editing and splits them into variants, so the calls hiding outside the test directory are found by search, not by a failing production build.

items.title: One pull request per batch
items.description: Roughly 25 files per PR, each linked to one tracking issue, each with the codemod path and the hand-patched files named in the body. Review a small diff and say go.

items.title: CI gates every batch
items.description: The next branch only starts after the previous PR lands green; the last batch runs the full suite, starts the app, then sweeps for dead config and leftover shims.

items.title: Connect once
items.description: The migration is coordinated through the Composio CLI: one login, then link your GitHub account for pull requests and CI status, and Linear (or Jira) for the tracking issue. Nothing is pushed before you approve the first batch.

items.title: State the change
items.description: Point at the repo and name what changes — framework version, old API, config format, or the boundary being moved. A failing test or a sample file pins the target.

items.title: Review the plan, not 200 files
items.description: You get the written transform, the file count, the tool choice and the batch order. Correct the rule here, where a fix costs one sentence.

items.title: Merge batch by batch
items.description: Each batch is its own branch and PR with the checks it passed. Approve, and the next batch rebases on top; progress lands as comments on the tracking issue.

blocks.title: What you need before the first batch
blocks.content: A GitHub account with push access to the target repo, and a Linear or Jira workspace for the tracking issue. Composio is installed and linked once; without it the migration still describes each transform correctly, but opens no PRs and records no CI verdict, so the review trail has to be assembled by hand.

blocks.title: It stops instead of guessing
blocks.content: If the search reaches thousands of files, if two transforms get tangled in one diff, or if a file resists every codemod, it reports that and asks — rather than inventing a rule that silently changes code you never pointed at. Rollback is per batch, so a branch that goes wrong is reverted alone.

## What it produces

- A written transform you can re-run or hand to a teammate.
- One tracking issue with a comment per batch, and roughly 25 files per pull request — each with its codemod, the checks that ran, and anything hand-patched.
- A closing report: what changed, what deliberately did not, how to verify it, and the residue list — dead config keys, disabled checks, compatibility shims, stale docs.

## Where it helps most

Framework upgrades that touch every import; API renames across a monorepo; test runner or bundler swaps; CommonJS to ESM; splitting a growing module into packages; and any long-postponed cleanup where the work is known but nobody wants the 8,000-line diff.

## What it will not do

Merge without you. Force-push a reviewed batch. Reformat files it did not otherwise touch — that only buries the real change. And when the scope is unclear it asks one question instead of choosing a cheap interpretation of “clean it up”.
